column1: What is the universal energy transducer molecule in muscle contraction, and what concentration range does it maintain at rest?
column2: ATP (adenosine triphosphate); maintained at roughly 4–6 mM in resting skeletal muscle, defended even during maximal exercise.

column1: Are the three ATP resynthesis pathways (PCr, glycolysis, oxidative phosphorylation) ever exclusively active in isolation during exercise?
column2: No — all three are always contributing to some degree; intensity and duration shift their relative contribution, not their on/off status.

column1: Compare the power output rate and capacity of the phosphocreatine system vs. oxidative phosphorylation.
column2: PCr system: highest ATP delivery rate (~36–40 mmol ATP·kg⁻¹ dry muscle·s⁻¹) but exhausted in 8–12 seconds. Oxidative phosphorylation: lowest rate but essentially capacity-unlimited due to abundant fat/carb substrate and sustainable O2 supply.

column1: State the Fick equation and define each term.
column2: VO2 = Cardiac Output × (a-vO2 diff). VO2 = oxygen consumption; Cardiac Output = HR × Stroke Volume; a-vO2 diff = arteriovenous oxygen difference (oxygen extracted by tissues).

column1: What causes the non-linear hyperventilation (ventilatory breakpoint) seen above the lactate threshold?
column2: Bicarbonate buffering of metabolically produced H+ ions generates excess CO2, which stimulates central chemoreceptors in the medulla, driving disproportionate increases in ventilation.

column1: How does the arteriovenous oxygen difference (a-vO2 diff) change from rest to maximal exercise?
column2: It rises from approximately 5 mL O2 per 100 mL blood at rest to 15–16 mL O2 per 100 mL blood at maximal exercise, due to capillary dilation and increased mitochondrial oxygen extraction.

column1: Define a motor unit and state Henneman's Size Principle.
column2: A motor unit = one alpha motor neuron plus all muscle fibers it innervates. The Size Principle states motor units are recruited in order from smallest/slowest-conducting (fatigue-resistant, low force) to largest/fastest-conducting (high force, fast fatigue) as demand increases.

column1: Contrast Type I, Type IIa, and Type IIx muscle fiber characteristics.
column2: Type I: high mitochondria/myoglobin, slow ATPase, high endurance, low force. Type IIa: hybrid, moderate oxidative + glycolytic capacity, burst power with some fatigue resistance. Type IIx: minimal mitochondria, high glycolytic flux, fastest ATPase, explosive force, rapid fatigue.

column1: Is muscle fiber type distribution fixed or plastic? What causes shifts between IIx and IIa?
column2: It is plastic. Chronic endurance training shifts fibers from IIx toward IIa; heavy resistance training and detraining can reverse this shift.

column1: What is the SAID principle and why is it foundational to exercise prescription?
column2: Specific Adaptation to Imposed Demand — the body adapts precisely to the specific mechanical, metabolic, or neural stimulus imposed, not generically; e.g., mitochondria proliferate only in fibers subjected to sustained metabolic flux, not those used for brief max-velocity efforts.

column1: What is the 'adaptive window' in training dose-response, and what happens outside its boundaries?
column2: The adaptive window is the training stimulus range between minimum effective dose and maximum recoverable volume. Below it: no structural remodeling occurs. Above it: regression occurs from accumulated fatigue outrunning repair.

column1: List the five interconnected categories of chronic training adaptation.
column2: 1) Mitochondrial biogenesis and density, 2) Skeletal muscle capillarization, 3) Structural cardiac remodeling, 4) Metabolic enzyme upregulation, 5) Nervous system refinement of motor unit recruitment.
